opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it in two layers.

The first layer is the foundation: the general capabilities that make an agent work at all. Planning over long horizons, recovering from mistakes, using tools reliably, knowing when it's uncertain. A lot of that comes from pretraining and post-training at scale, and especially from reinforcement learning. RL is really the key ingredient. Pretraining gives you a model that knows a lot about the world. RL is what teaches it to act in the world toward a goal. The lesson I took from my time working on systems like AlphaGo and later on Gemini is that once you have a strong prior, RL lets you go well beyond imitation. The model starts finding strategies nobody showed it.

The second layer, which I think gets underappreciated, is the specific capabilities a particular end user actually needs. A generally capable agent isn't automatically useful to someone doing their real job. Usefulness comes from depth in a domain: understanding the context, the tools, the workflows, and what "good" looks like for that person. So we try to be very concrete. We pick a domain, work closely with the people who'll use the agent, and build environments and evaluations that reflect the real tasks they do, not toy benchmarks.

The hardest part is usually the reward signal. In Go, you know who won. In real-world work, "did the agent do a good job" is fuzzy. A big part of the craft is building reliable ways to measure success. That might be verifiable checks where you can get them, learned reward models where you can't, and a lot of human feedback early on to calibrate both. If your evals and rewards are good, the training tends to follow. If they're off, you'll optimize very efficiently toward the wrong thing.

So my short answer is: build broad agentic capability with RL, then go deep on a real user's problem, and spend a disproportionate amount of effort on defining and measuring what success looks like. That's where most of the leverage is.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it as a loop between the environment and the model, and the environment is the part people underestimate. When we started Reflection, the thing we kept coming back to is that the capabilities you want in an agent are almost never the ones you get for free from pretraining. Pretraining gives you a model that knows a lot and can talk about anything, but being useful to an end user means something more specific: it means finishing a multi-step task, recovering when a tool call fails, knowing when to stop and ask versus push through. Those are behaviors, not facts, and you don't get behaviors from reading the internet.

So the first question we ask is, what does the user actually need done? Not in the abstract, but concretely: if you watch an engineer for a day, what are the tasks they hand off, what does success look like, and how do you know when it's done? That last piece matters most because it's what turns a vague wish into something you can train on. If you can verify the outcome, you can build a reward, and once you have a reward you can run reinforcement learning at scale. Coding is the obvious case: the code runs or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. That's why coding agents moved first.

The second thing is that the environment has to be realistic. There's a temptation to train on clean, synthetic tasks because they're easy to set up, and then you deploy and the agent falls over the moment it hits a messy repo or a flaky API. We spend a lot of effort making the training distribution look like the deployment distribution, including the failures. An agent that has never seen a broken build during training will not handle one gracefully in production.

Then there's a cultural piece. In my experience, from DeepMind and from working on Gemini, the teams that made real progress treated research and product as one problem. The product tells you what to measure, and the research tells you how to move it. If those are separate groups passing documents back and forth, you lose months. So we keep the people building evals, the people building environments, and the people training the model very close together, ideally the same people.

And honestly, the last thing is patience with the boring parts. Most of the work is building infrastructure: sandboxes, verifiers, data pipelines, ways to inspect thousands of agent trajectories and see where things went wrong. It's not glamorous, but it's where the capability actually comes from. The algorithm is a smaller piece of the puzzle than people assume.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with what the user is actually trying to accomplish and work backward. A useful agent needs more than the ability to give a good answer. It needs to take actions, observe what happened, and adjust when something doesn’t go according to plan.

So the training problem is really: can you put the model in environments where it can practice that whole loop, and give it a signal about whether it accomplished the task? If you only train individual steps, you can get something that looks competent locally but doesn’t reliably finish the job.

And then there’s a question of what you reward. Did it actually solve the user’s problem? Did it check its work? Did it ask for clarification when it needed to? Those are all parts of being useful. The goal is to train toward successful outcomes across a range of tasks, so the agent learns behaviors that transfer when a user asks it to do something it hasn’t seen before.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with what the user actually wants accomplished and work backward. A useful agent needs more than the ability to give a good answer. It needs to take actions, observe what happened, and keep making progress toward a goal. And when something goes wrong, it needs to recognize that and recover.

That changes how you think about training. You want environments where the model can practice doing complete tasks and get feedback on whether it succeeded. If the task is to find some information and put it into a spreadsheet, did it find the right information? Did it put it in the right place? Did it actually finish? Those are much more useful signals than whether an individual response sounded plausible.

The challenge is making that training generalize. You don’t want an agent that has memorized one workflow. You want it to learn how to explore an unfamiliar interface, check its work, and adapt when its first approach fails. So I’d think about capabilities in terms of the behaviors that let an agent reliably complete tasks, and then build training around practicing those behaviors across a broad range of situations.
